title: Signals, queries, conditions and timers

story: Monday, 09:25. Nova posts its plan for RH-1234 in the ticket's Slack thread, with three buttons: Approve, Change and Stop. The VM that wrote the plan has already been released. But you left for a long weekend at 09:10, so nobody presses anything until Thursday.

The run now has three things to wait for at the same time: your click, which should start the build the moment it comes; one day passing, so Nova can remind you; and three days passing, so Nova can hand the ticket back to you. A loop that checks a database every minute would cost something every minute, and a setTimeout would die with the next deploy.
hook.question: How does a run wait three days for one click, react the moment it comes, and remind you if it does not?

p: When you press Approve, the Slack app, our small service that turns Slack actions into messages for runs, sends a signal to the run. A signal is a named message that a client sends to one open run, which it finds by the workflow ID. The Temporal Service writes the signal into the run's history before anything else happens, so it is safe even when no worker is running at that moment: the next worker that handles the run delivers it.

Inside the workflow you declare the signal with defineSignal and attach a handler with setHandler. The handler does one small job: it stores the decision in a variable. It does not call activities and does not wait for anything, because the body of the workflow does the real work once it sees the new value. The button also carries the plan's version, so a click on an old message cannot approve a newer plan.

notes.text: The signal's name and the type of its message. The Slack app and the workflow import the same definition.
The handler only stores the decision. Set handlers at the top, before the first await.
A query handler only reads. The last section explains why.
A handle by workflow ID is enough. The signal reaches whichever run of nova:RH-1234 is open.

read.h: condition(): wait until it is true, or until time runs out
p: Now the workflow has to wait until decision has a value. condition(fn) does exactly that: it waits until fn returns true, and Temporal checks fn again every time something happens in the run, such as a signal arriving. With a timeout as the second argument it gives back a boolean: true if fn became true in time, false if the time ran out first. The timeout is a durable timer, kept by the Temporal Service like sleep in the first lesson, so a three-day wait survives every deploy, and while it waits, no code runs.

Two calls to condition give us the whole rule for a plan: wait one day, remind, wait two more days, hand the ticket back. Our platform keeps that rule in one helper, so every wait on a person behaves the same way.

The history at the end of this section shows how cheap this is. It comes from a lab run where you approved within a few seconds: one timer, one signal, and the timer is cancelled because nobody needs it any more. Three days of waiting would look the same, with a longer gap between the lines.

notes.text: Waits up to one day. If you click within that day, it returns true at once, and the run continues.
The day passed with no click, so Nova reminds you once, in the thread and on Jira.
Two days after the reminder, the ticket goes back to you, and the run ends as parked.

read.see:
$ temporal workflow show -w nova:RH-1234 | grep -v WorkflowTask
    1  WorkflowExecutionStarted
    7  ActivityTaskCompleted        ← the plan was posted
   11  TimerStarted                 ← the reminder timer of condition()
   12  WorkflowExecutionSignaled    ← you pressed Approve
   16  TimerCanceled                ← the timer is no longer needed
   17  WorkflowExecutionCompleted

p: When you type /nova status RH-1234, Slack must answer without disturbing the run. That is a query: a named question that a worker answers from the run's current state, at that moment. A query is not written to the history, so its handler must only read. If it changed a variable, the change would disappear on the next replay, because nothing recorded it.

There is one more difference, and it matters during an outage. A signal is stored by the Temporal Service, so it is accepted even when every worker is down. A query is answered by a worker, so with no worker running it waits and then fails. In the lab you stop the worker and see both: the approval is accepted, and the status question fails.
read.see:
$ temporal workflow signal -w nova:RH-1236 --name decidePlan --input '{"kind":"approve","by":"sean"}'
Signal workflow succeeded
$ temporal workflow query -w nova:RH-1236 --name status
Error: querying workflow failed: query timed out before a worker could process it

deeper.h: Go deeper: the question loop, and a cheaper VM while people think
p: Questions during the build use the same tools. When Nova asks something, workInSandbox returns with needsAnswer, and the workflow waits for the answerQuestion signal. Most answers come within minutes, so the VM stays on for 10 minutes. After that the workflow parks the VM: it stops the machine and keeps its disk, which costs almost nothing. When the answer arrives, it wakes the VM and the same session continues with your reply.
Temporal also has updates, a message that changes the run and returns a result to the sender. Our platform does not use them: signals for changes and one status query cover what Slack and Jira need.

lab.title: Approve a waiting run, or let it park
needs: The p7-1 lab folder, for worker.mjs and start.mjs
lab.goal: Make a run wait for a plan decision with a reminder and a time limit, send the decision as a signal, and read the run's state with a query.

guess.q: The run waits with condition(() => decision !== undefined, '20 seconds'). Five seconds after it starts, you send the decidePlan signal. When does the run continue?

options.text: After the full 20 seconds, when the timer fires.
options.why: That is what sleep would do. condition checks the function again when the signal arrives, so it does not wait for the timer.

options.text: Right away, and the 20-second timer is cancelled.
options.why: The signal sets decision, Temporal checks the condition again, it is true, and the timer is no longer needed. The history shows TimerCanceled.

options.text: Never, because the signal arrived while the workflow was waiting and was lost.
options.why: Signals are recorded in the history first, so they are never lost, even with no worker running.

follow.say: Keep the dev server running from the last lab, or start it again in the first tab.

Write the workflow: a signal for the decision, a query for the status, and two waits with condition. The drill times are seconds: 20 before the reminder, 40 more before it parks.

# now press Ctrl+C in the worker tab
temporal workflow signal -w nova:RH-1236 --name decidePlan --input '{"kind":"approve","by":"sean"}'
temporal workflow query -w nova:RH-1236 --name status
follow.see:
Signal workflow succeeded
Error: querying workflow failed: query timed out before a worker could process it

follow.do:

# third tab
temporal workflow result -w nova:RH-1236
follow.see:

lab.build: Add a Stop button. Define a second signal, stop, whose message is the name of the person who stopped the run, and store it in a variable. Change both waits so that a Stop ends them at once, just like a decision does, and make the run return "stopped by <name>" with the status Stopped. Restart the worker, start a run for RH-1237 and stop it with temporal workflow signal -w nova:RH-1237 --name stop --input '"sean"'.
checks: The query for nova:RH-1234 answered "Awaiting approval" before you sent the signal.
The history of nova:RH-1234 shows WorkflowExecutionSignaled followed by TimerCanceled.
nova:RH-1235 printed one reminder and ended with the result "parked", without any signal.
With the worker stopped, the signal for nova:RH-1236 succeeded and the query failed; after the restart the result was "approve by sean".
For your build: temporal workflow result -w nova:RH-1237 shows "stopped by sean" within a second or two of the signal, not after the timers.
lab.fix: A teammate found condition hard to read and rewrote the wait with plain timers: await sleep('20 seconds'), then if (!decision) send the reminder and await sleep('40 seconds'), then park if there is still no decision. It looks the same, and the reminder still works. But today you approved a plan five minutes after it was posted, /nova status kept saying Awaiting approval, and Nova started the build only a day later. Make that change, start a run for RH-1300, approve it at once, and see the result arrive only when the first timer fires. Then put condition back.
explain: Why can a run wait three days for a click without costing anything, and where is the timer during that time?
Why does the decision reach the run when no worker is running, while the status question fails?
Why must a query handler only read, and never change a variable?
lab.done: A run continued the moment it got the decidePlan signal, another one reminded and parked on its own, the approval survived a stopped worker, and you stopped the worker and the dev server.

check.q: The plan waits with condition(() => decision !== undefined, 1 day). You press Approve after 10 minutes. What happens to the one-day timer?

options.text: It is cancelled, and the run continues at once
options.why: The signal sets decision, Temporal checks the condition again, and since it is true the timer is no longer needed.

options.text: It keeps running, and the run continues when it fires
options.why: That is how sleep followed by a check behaves. condition reacts to the signal immediately.

options.text: It restarts, so the next reminder is a day after your click
options.why: Nothing restarts. You decided, so there is nothing left to remind you about.

check.q: All orchestrator workers are down for ten minutes. You press Approve in Slack, then type /nova status RH-1234. What happens?

options.text: Both fail until a worker comes back
options.why: The signal does not need a worker: the Temporal Service records it in the history right away.

options.text: Both work, because the Temporal Service answers both
options.why: The service never runs your code, and the status comes from a query handler in your code, so a worker must answer it.

options.text: The approval is recorded and delivered later; the status query waits and then fails
options.why: Signals are stored by the service. Queries are computed by a worker from the run's state, so they need a live worker.

check.q: A teammate wants the status query handler to count how often people ask, with asked += 1. Why is that a bad idea?

options.text: Queries are not recorded in the history, so the count is lost on the next replay
options.why: A replay rebuilds state from the history only. Anything a query changed is not there, so the workflow would see different values.

options.text: Query handlers cannot read variables of the workflow
options.why: They can read them; reading the run's state is exactly their job.

options.text: Every query adds an event to the history, so the history grows too fast
options.why: It is the other way round: queries add nothing to the history. That is why they must not change anything.

p: ticketToPr accepts three signals, decidePlan from the plan buttons, answerQuestion from a reply in the ticket's thread and stop from the Stop button or /nova stop, and one query, status, for /nova status. Only the requester's decision counts; anyone else who clicks is told that only the requester can decide this plan.

Every wait on a person goes through waitForPerson, with fixed times: a plan is reminded after 1 day and parked after 3, a question is reminded after 1 day and parked after 2, a PR review after 2 days and closed with a note after 14. Drill tickets use the same numbers in minutes. A parked ticket goes back to the requester, and a later assignment starts a fresh run with the same ID.

tickets.why: ticketToPr's signals and its status query, and the question loop that parks the VM while a person thinks.
waitForPerson: remind, then park, with durable timers for every wait on a person.
The Slack buttons that send decidePlan, with the plan version on each button.

words.plain: A named message a client sends to one open run. Temporal records it, so it is never lost.
The small function in the workflow that runs when a signal arrives. It only changes state.
Waits until a function returns true, optionally with a timeout; gives back false if the time ran out.
A timer kept by the Temporal Service, so it fires even if every worker restarted in between.
A question a worker answers from the run's current state. It is not recorded and must not change anything.

review.q: Write the two condition calls that remind after one day and park after three.
review.a: if (await condition(done, 1 day)) continue; else notify; then if (await condition(done, 2 days)) continue; else park. The second wait is two days, because one has already passed.

review.q: Why does the Slack app use a signal for Approve and a query for /nova status?
review.a: Approve changes the run, so it must be recorded and must survive an outage: a signal. Status only reads the current state and must not change anything: a query.

review.q: What is wrong with sleep(1 day) followed by if (!decision)?
review.a: The run does not react to the click until the timer fires, so an approval can wait a whole day. condition with a timeout continues the moment the condition is true.

remember: A signal records the click, condition waits for it with a durable timer as the deadline, and a query only reads.
